findings.explanation: At line 299, both `key` and `value` are interpolated directly into a SQLAlchemy `text()` expression via Python string formatting: `text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.{} == \"{}\")')".format(key, value))`. This is inside the Oracle-specific branch of the JSON column filter logic. Neither `key` nor `value` is passed as a bound parameter — they are embedded raw into the SQL string. `key` originates from the filter's key field (user-controlled filter input) and `value` is the user-supplied filter value. Although there is a prior check that `oper == operator.eq` and that the value contains no wildcards (`*` or `%`), there is no whitelist validation of `key` against known safe identifiers, and no sanitization of `value` against characters such as single-quotes, backslashes, or other SQL meta-characters. A crafted `key` like `x == 1) OR 1=1 --` or a `value` containing a single quote could break out of the JSON path expression and inject arbitrary SQL. The correct fix is to use SQLAlchemy bound parameters (`:key` / `:value`) rather than string interpolation.

findings.suggested_fix:
Use SQLAlchemy named bound parameters instead of Python string formatting. For example:

```python
expression = text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@." + key_safe + " == \":val\")')").bindparams(val=value)
```
Where `key_safe` is validated against a strict whitelist of known JSON metadata attribute names (e.g., checked against the model's allowed metadata keys). The `value` should be passed exclusively as a bound parameter so the database driver handles escaping, preventing injection via either argument.
findings.semgrep_message: SQLAlchemy text()/exec_driver_sql() with dynamic content may allow SQL injection if user input is interpolated. Verify that only bound parameters are used.

findings.explanation: In both `list_dids` (line 77) and `list_dids_extended` (line 109) in the PR, when a filter group contains a `scope` key, the internalized `InternalScope` value is incorrectly stored under the `account` key (`or_group['account'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)`) instead of `or_group['scope']`. This means: (1) the `scope` filter is never VO-namespaced — it remains as a raw external string — allowing the core query layer (`did.list_dids` / `did.list_dids_extended`) to receive an un-internalized scope value that is not bound to the caller's VO, and (2) any legitimate `account` filter already stored in `or_group['account']` from the earlier branch is silently overwritten with a scope object. The net effect is that the VO-isolation enforcement on the `scope` filter is broken: a caller can supply a scope belonging to a different VO and the API layer will pass it through to the database query without binding it to the requesting VO, potentially exposing DIDs from other VOs. The base code correctly set `filters['scope'] = InternalScope(filters['scope'], vo=vo)` (base lines 106–107), but the PR replaces this with the wrong key assignment.
findings.suggested_fix: Change `or_group['account'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)` to `or_group['scope'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)` in both `list_dids` (line 77) and `list_dids_extended` (line 109) so that the scope filter is VO-namespaced and stored under the correct key, matching the correct behavior from the base code.

findings.explanation: The PR changes DID_FILTERS from a strict JSON Schema (type: object, with only 'created_before'/'created_after' date properties allowed) to an unrestricted array schema (type: array, additionalProperties: true) across all nine VO-specific schema files. The `validate_schema` call at `lib/rucio/api/did.py:101` is the sole input-validation gate before user-supplied filter keys are passed into `FilterEngine`, which then coerces arbitrary string keys to SQLAlchemy model attributes via `hasattr`/`getattr` on `models.DataIdentifier` (filter_engine.py:87-88). With the old schema, only known date fields were permitted; with the new schema, any key/value pairs in any array element pass schema validation unchecked. This is an incorrect authorization control: the schema that is supposed to constrain what filter attributes a user may query against internal data model columns has been effectively removed, allowing users to probe or filter on any column attribute of `DataIdentifier` (including internal fields such as `purged_replicas`, `bytes`, `md5`, `adler32`, `is_open`, `suppressed`, etc.) that they should not be able to enumerate or filter by. The existing check that should prevent unauthorized attribute access is thus bypassed.

findings.suggested_fix: Restore a restrictive JSON Schema for DID_FILTERS that enumerates only the permitted filter keys (e.g., 'name', 'scope', 'did_type', 'created_before', 'created_after', and any explicitly approved metadata keys). The schema items should be typed objects with an explicit allowlist of properties and `additionalProperties: false`, so that users cannot inject arbitrary model column names as filter keys.

findings.explanation: The PR changes DID_FILTERS schema from a typed object (with only 'created_before'/'created_after' date properties) to an untyped array with 'additionalProperties: True'. This is the only validation gate before filter keys and values reach SQL. In create_sqla_query(), at line 299, when a filter key cannot be coerced to a model attribute and json_column is set (Oracle path), both the key and value are interpolated directly into a raw SQL text() expression via Python string formatting: `text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.{} == \"{}\")')".format(key, value))`. Before this PR, schema validation would reject arbitrary keys/values for all VOs. After this PR, the schema accepts any array element with any keys and values (type:array, additionalProperties:true), so an attacker can supply arbitrary strings for both the filter key name and value that flow unescaped into the Oracle json_exists SQL expression.

findings.suggested_fix: The DID_FILTERS schema should define an array of objects where each item's keys are restricted to a known allowlist of valid metadata field names (e.g., using 'enum' on property names or 'additionalProperties: false' with explicit properties), and values should be typed appropriately. Additionally, in create_sqla_query(), the Oracle json_exists expression should use bound parameters instead of string formatting for both the key (validated against an allowlist) and the value.

findings.explanation: In the PR's filter_engine.py at line 299, the Oracle code path inside create_sqla_query uses Python string formatting to embed both `key` (a user-supplied metadata filter key that could not be coerced to a model attribute) and `value` (a user-supplied filter value) directly into a raw SQL text() expression: `text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.{} == \"{}\")')".format(key, value))`. When json_meta.py calls FilterEngine with strict_coerce=False (as introduced by this PR), keys that are not model attributes remain as raw strings and flow into this Oracle branch. Neither `key` nor `value` is bound as a parameter or validated against an allowlist before being interpolated into the SQL string. An attacker who controls filter keys or values (e.g. via the list_dids API) can inject arbitrary Oracle SQL through either the key name or the value string.
findings.suggested_fix: Use Oracle's JSON_EXISTS bind variable syntax rather than string interpolation. The key (JSON path element) should be validated against a strict allowlist of permitted metadata key names. The value should be passed as a bind parameter using SQLAlchemy's bindparam() mechanism. For example: `text("json_exists(meta, '$?(@." + safe_key + " == $val)')").bindparams(val=value)` after validating `key` against an allowlist, or restructure to use Oracle's native JSON path bind variable support.

findings.explanation: The new `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute` helper (lines 76-92, PR snapshot) resolves user-supplied filter key strings directly against any SQLAlchemy model class using `hasattr` / `getattr`. When `strict=True` it rejects unknown keys, but the check is purely membership-based: any attribute that happens to exist on the model class (including internal/sensitive columns like `account`, `availability`, `monotonic`, `obsolete`, `suppressed`, etc.) is silently accepted and mapped to a query filter. The `manages_key` guard in `did_column_meta.py` (lines 286-313) maintains an explicit exclusion list of sensitive columns (`account`, `availability`, `complete`, `is_open`, `monotonic`, `obsolete`, `suppressed`, `updated_at`), but that guard is only consulted by the plugin dispatch layer — it is not enforced inside `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute`. An attacker who can supply raw filter dictionaries directly to `FilterEngine.__init__` (e.g. via internal API callers that pass `strict_coerce=False` or that use `model_class` directly) can reference those excluded sensitive columns as filter keys, potentially leaking rows they are not supposed to see or fingerprinting internal state (IDOR via unintended column exposure). The PR replaces a hardcoded-allowlist approach with a purely dynamic `hasattr` check, widening the attack surface compared to the base.

findings.explanation: The new `manages_key` implementation dynamically builds the allowed key set by calling `inspect(models.DataIdentifier).attrs` and then subtracting an `exclude_did_table_columns` list. The old code used a static `HARDCODED_KEYS` allowlist. The new dynamic approach means that if a new internal/sensitive column is ever added to the `DataIdentifier` model (e.g. a column tracking internal account or security metadata), it will automatically become an allowed filter key unless the developer remembers to also add it to `exclude_did_table_columns`. Additionally, comparing the new `exclude_did_table_columns` against the old `HARDCODED_KEYS`, several columns that were never in the old allowlist (e.g. `name`, `bytes`, `md5`, `adler32`, `expired_at`, `deleted_at`, `events`, `guid`, `purge_replicas`, `hidden`, `is_new`, `accessed_at`, `closed_at`, `eol_at`, `is_archive`, `constituent`, `access_cnt`, `task_id`, `panda_id`, `lumiblocknr`, `provenance`, `phys_group`, `transient`) are now exposed through `manages_key` returning `True` — including internal/sensitive columns such as `purge_replicas`, `obsolete` is excluded but `deleted_at` and `expired_at` are not excluded, which means those internal lifecycle columns can now be used as filter criteria. More critically, the `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute` method in the new `FilterEngine` uses `hasattr(model_class, word)` / `getattr(model_class, word)` on user-supplied keys (line 87-88) without any column allowlist check, so any column attribute of `models.DataIdentifier` reachable via `hasattr` can be used to filter the SQL query. The new `list_dids` feeds user-controlled filter keys directly into `FilterEngine` without pre-validating them against `manages_key`, meaning the `exclude_did_table_columns` exclusion list in `manages_key` is never consulted in the `list_dids` query-building path. This is an incorrect authorization check: the exclusion list exists to protect certain columns but is bypassed in the main query path.

findings.suggested_fix: The `list_dids` method should validate user-supplied filter keys against the `manages_key` allowlist (or an equivalent explicit column allowlist) before passing them to `FilterEngine`. Alternatively, `FilterEngine._coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute` should be given an explicit allowlist of permitted column names to restrict what columns can be used in filter queries, rather than accepting any attribute that `hasattr` returns true for. The `exclude_did_table_columns` list in `manages_key` should also be reviewed to ensure all sensitive/internal columns (such as `deleted_at`, `expired_at`) are excluded from user-controlled filtering.

findings.explanation: The `delete_metadata` function in `lib/rucio/api/did.py` (lines 556-569) does not perform any authorization check before deleting metadata. It only converts the scope to an InternalScope and directly calls `did.delete_metadata()`. In contrast, `set_metadata` (line 463) and `set_metadata_bulk` (line 489) both call `rucio.api.permission.has_permission()` before proceeding. This missing authorization check at the API layer means any authenticated user can delete metadata keys from any DID, regardless of ownership or role. This is a pre-existing gap in the base code, but the PR's refactor of the core plugin layer (`did_meta_plugins/__init__.py`) now routes `delete_metadata` through multiple plugins via the new `METADATA_PLUGIN_MODULES` list, potentially expanding the scope of keys deletable without authorization (previously only keys managed by the single configured handler were reachable).

So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3

Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

[etc/docker/dev/README.rst:102-143] (relevance 0.10)
Then you will have to run the transfer daemons (conveyor-\*) and messaging daemon (hermes) to send the events to ActiveMQ. There a script for that which repeats these daemons in single execution mode from the section in a loop::

    run_daemons


When all the daemons ran you will be able to find the events in Kibana. If you run the docker environment on you local machine you can access Kibana at http://localhost:5601. The necessary index pattern will be added automatically. There is also one dashboard available in Kibana. If it is running on remote machine you can SSH forward it::

    ssh -L 5601:127.0.0.1:5601 <hostname>


Additionally, there is also a Grafana server running with one simple dashboard. You can access it at http://localhost:3000. The default credentials are "admin/admin". Also ActiveMQ web console can be accessed at http://localhost:8161.

If you would like to continously create some transfers and events there are scripts available for that. Open two different shells and in one run::

    create_monit_data


And in the other run::

    run_daemons


Development
-----------

The idea for containerised development is that you use your host machine to edit the files, and test the changes within the container environment. Any change to files in your clone will be reflected into the containers by using volume mounts.

To see your changes in action the recommended way is to jump twice into the container in parallel. One terminal to follow the output of the Rucio server with a shortcut to tail the logfiles (`logshow`), and one terminal to actually run interactive commands:

From your host, get a separate Terminal 1 (the Rucio "server log show")::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash
    logshow


Terminal 1 can now be left open, and then from your host go into a new Terminal 2 (the "interactive" terminal)::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash
    rucio whoami


The command will output in Terminal 2, and at the same time the server debug output will be shown in Terminal 1.

Now, ensure that the `.git/config` is proper, i.e., mentioning your full name and email address, and create the `.githubtoken` file that contains a full access token from `Github Account Settings <https://github.com/settings/tokens>`_.

Next, startup the Rucio development environment with docker-compose. There are three different types: a standard one to just run the unittests and do basic development, which includes just Rucio without any transfer capabilities. One slightly larger one, which includes the File Transfer Service (FTS) and three XrootD storage servers to develop upload/download and transfers capabilities. And a third large one, which adds the full monitoring stack with Logstash, Elasticsearch, Kibana and Grafana.

*Note: if you are running with SELinux enabled, you might run into problems. Check troubleshooting with SELinux on the help pages of your container runtime environment.*

Using the standard environment
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Run the containers using docker-compose (again might need `sudo`)::

    docker-compose --file etc/docker/dev/docker-compose.yml up -d

And verify that it is running properly::

    docker ps

This should show you a few running containers: the Rucio server, the PostgreSQL database and the Graphite monitoring.

Finally, you can jump into the container with::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash

To verify that everything is in order, you can now either run the full unit tests or only set up the database. Running the full testing suite takes ~10 minutes::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh

Alternatively, you can bootstrap the test environment once with the `-i` option and then selectively or repeatedly run test case modules, test case groups, or even single test cases, for example::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh -i
    tools/pytest.sh test_replica.py
    tools/pytest.sh -vvv test_replica.py::TestReplicaCore
    tools/pytest.sh -vvv --full-trace test_replica.py::TestReplicaCore::test_delete_replicas_from_datasets

Now, ensure that the `.git/config` is proper, i.e., mentioning your full name and email address, and create the `.githubtoken` file that contains a full access token from `Github Account Settings <https://github.com/settings/tokens>`_.

Next, startup the Rucio development environment with docker-compose. There are three different types: a standard one to just run the unittests and do basic development, which includes just Rucio without any transfer capabilities. One slightly larger one, which includes the File Transfer Service (FTS) and three XrootD storage servers to develop upload/download and transfers capabilities. And a third large one, which adds the full monitoring stack with Logstash, Elasticsearch, Kibana and Grafana.

*Note: if you are running with SELinux enabled, you might run into problems. Check troubleshooting with SELinux on the help pages of your container runtime environment.*

Using the standard environment
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Run the containers using docker-compose (again might need `sudo`)::

    docker-compose --file etc/docker/dev/docker-compose.yml up -d

And verify that it is running properly::

    docker ps

This should show you a few running containers: the Rucio server, the PostgreSQL database and the Graphite monitoring.

Finally, you can jump into the container with::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash

To verify that everything is in order, you can now either run the full unit tests or only set up the database. Running the full testing suite takes ~10 minutes::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh

Alternatively, you can bootstrap the test environment once with the `-i` option and then selectively or repeatedly run test case modules, test case groups, or even single test cases, for example::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh -i
    tools/pytest.sh test_replica.py
    tools/pytest.sh -vvv test_replica.py::TestReplicaCore

If you run the command below, the files are not in the RSE XRD3, but only in XRD1 and 2.::

    rucio list-file-replicas test:mynewdataset
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+
    > | SCOPE   | NAME   | FILESIZE   | ADLER32   | RSE: REPLICA                                   |
    > |---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------|
    > | test    | file1  | 10.486 MB  | 141a641e  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/80/25/file1 |
    > | test    | file2  | 10.486 MB  | fdfa7eea  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/f3/14/file2 |
    > | test    | file3  | 10.486 MB  | c669167d  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/a9/23/file3 |
    > | test    | file4  | 10.486 MB  | 65786e49  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/2b/c2/file4 |
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+


So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. After that, the transfer state check daemon (conveyor-poller) will retrieve from FTS the transfer state information. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-submitter --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-poller --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-finisher --run-once

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.04)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.10)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.06)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.
